claims.baseline: unstructured interacting group (the contrast the features were designed against)
claims.effect_size: definitional (4 named features; not a measured contrast)
claims.locator: opening section 'Four necessary features characterize a Delphi procedure'

source_lineage.title: Expert opinions in forecasting: The role of the Delphi technique

claims.strongest_caveat: This is a definitional package, not an isolated causal test of each feature. RAND RM-5888-PR (Dalkey 1969, doi:10.7249/RM5888) is the experimental origin but its PDF was not retrievable this session (HTTP 404 on the RAND product path), so no Dalkey cell count promotes a mechanism.
claims.text: A Delphi procedure is defined by four operational features: anonymity of panelists, iteration over rounds, controlled feedback of the panel's judgments between rounds, and statistical aggregation of the group response.

claims.baseline: unstructured traditional / interacting groups (same review set)
claims.effect_size: Delphi outperformed traditional groups 5 studies to 1, with 2 ties, and 1 task-specific mixed result (Rowe and Wright 1999 synthesis restated in this chapter)
claims.locator: section 'When the alternative is a traditional group'

source_lineage.title: Expert opinions in forecasting: The role of the Delphi technique

claims.strongest_caveat: The chapter abstract states 'five to one with one tie' while the body states 'five studies to one, with two ties, and with one study showing task-specific support for both techniques'. Lab panels are usually students; Graefe and Armstrong (2011) found the same directional MAE advantage (5.62 vs 7.21) that was not statistically significant overall (Kruskal-Wallis ns). Study-count is not a Cohen's d.
claims.text: Iteration plus controlled feedback, taken as the Delphi package versus an unstructured traditional group, has a study-count advantage on accuracy.

claims.baseline: face-to-face overall MAE 7.21 (NGT 5.92; prediction markets 7.07); Kruskal-Wallis ns across four methods
claims.effect_size: Delphi overall MAE 5.62; significantly better than FTF on 2 of 10 questions; never significantly worse
claims.locator: section 'Relative accuracy of group methods' / Conclusion

source_lineage.title: Comparing face-to-face meetings, nominal groups, Delphi and prediction markets on an estimation task

claims.strongest_caveat: Directional MAE advantage does not survive the overall Kruskal-Wallis test. Task was factual percentage estimates without distributed private knowledge. This row therefore cannot carry the unstructured-group comparison alone; it is a contradiction/qualification edge on R2.
claims.text: On one laboratory estimation task with 227 participants (11 groups per method), Delphi mean absolute error was lower than face-to-face meetings, but the four-method overall test was not statistically significant.

claims.baseline: first-round Delphi aggregates or independent statistical (non-interacting) groups
claims.effect_size: Delphi vs first-round or statistical groups 12 studies to 2, with 2 ties; 5 of the 12 reported statistically significant accuracy gains over rounds
claims.locator: section 'When the alternative is simply to average the forecasts of several individuals'

source_lineage.title: Expert opinions in forecasting: The role of the Delphi technique

claims.strongest_caveat: Two studies found Delphi worse (Gustafson et al. 1973: worse than first-round on 7/8 items and vs independent statistical groups on 6/8; Boje and Murnighan 1982: worse over rounds on 3/4 items). Erffmeyer 1984 and 1986 may double-count the same dataset. First-round Delphi is not a pure statistical-group control because panelists expect later feedback.
claims.text: Iteration plus controlled feedback, taken as Delphi versus a one-round statistical aggregate of the same or comparable individuals, has a study-count accuracy advantage.

claims.baseline: not reported (no anonymous-vs-identified accuracy table in this source)
claims.effect_size: none isolated (rationale only; cites Dalkey 1972)
claims.locator: section discussing subject anonymity as a primary characteristic

source_lineage.title: The Delphi Technique: Making Sense of Consensus

claims.strongest_caveat: Headline 'anonymity reduces dominance' without a measured baseline is E3 and cannot promote the mechanism. Boulkedid et al. 2011 further show the rule is frequently dropped in practice (modified Delphi with a physical meeting).
claims.text: Anonymity is a named necessary feature of classical Delphi, justified as reducing dominance and conformity pressure, but this session found no isolated contrast (anonymous vs identified under otherwise identical iteration and feedback) that reports an effect size and a baseline.

claims.baseline: 98 studies whose aim was consensus (of 100 sampled Delphi studies)
claims.effect_size: 48/100 two rounds; 42/100 three rounds; 70/98 (71.4%) stopped for number of rounds vs 23/98 (23.5%) stopped for consensus
claims.locator: Table 2 (rounds) and Table 3 (reason to stop)

source_lineage.title: Defining consensus: A systematic review recommends methodologic criteria for reporting of Delphi studies

claims.strongest_caveat: These are observational reporting counts, not a causal test that 2-3 rounds maximises accuracy. The row therefore supports 'this is how Delphi is run' (convention in use) rather than 'this round count is optimal'.
claims.text: Two or three rounds is the conventional stopping rule. In a random sample of 100 Delphi studies (2000-2009), 48 finished in 2 rounds and 42 in 3; 70 of 98 consensus-aiming studies stopped because a planned round count was reached, not because consensus was measured.

claims.baseline: 72 of 98 consensus-aiming studies that provided any consensus definition
claims.effect_size: percent agreement used in 25 of 72 studies that defined consensus; median threshold 75% (range 50-97%) among percentage/proportion definitions that stated a cut-off
claims.locator: Table 4 and Results section 3.3

source_lineage.title: Defining consensus: A systematic review recommends methodologic criteria for reporting of Delphi studies

claims.strongest_caveat: A 75% cut-off is the median of arbitrary thresholds, not a calibrated operating point. Authors concluded consensus was reached in 86/98 studies, but an a priori threshold existed in only 42 of those 86.
claims.text: Percent agreement is the most common consensus definition; when a percentage/proportion threshold is stated, the median cut-off is 75% (range 50-97%). That median is a reporting convention, not a validated accuracy optimum.

claims.baseline: not reported for the aggregation-statistic choice (the 12-to-2 tally contrasts the whole Delphi package with a statistical group, not median with mean)
claims.effect_size: none isolated for median vs mean
claims.locator: procedure description: 'the facilitator takes the group judgment as the statistical average (mean or median) of the panelists' estimates on the final round'

source_lineage.title: Expert opinions in forecasting: The role of the Delphi technique

claims.strongest_caveat: Using a group statistic is part of the package that beat unstructured groups in R2/R3; the specific choice of median versus mean is convention. Headline 'use the median' without a median-vs-mean baseline cannot promote.
claims.text: The group answer is taken as a statistical summary (mean or median) of the final-round estimates rather than a spokesperson outcome. Median-plus-quartiles is conventional; this session did not isolate median vs mean with an effect size and baseline.

claims.baseline: 80 included healthcare quality-indicator Delphi studies
claims.effect_size: 48/80 (60%) reported that feedback was given between rounds; of those, 28/48 (58%) quantitative only, 19/48 (40%) quantitative+qualitative, 1/48 (2%) qualitative; individual feedback reported in 31/80 (39%)
claims.locator: Table 4 Feedback rows; Results 'Data on the Progress of the Delphi Procedure'

source_lineage.authors: Boulkedid R, Abdoul H, Loustau M, Sibony O, Alberti C
source_lineage.title: Using and reporting the Delphi method for selecting healthcare quality indicators: A systematic review

claims.strongest_caveat: These are reporting rates, not a causal ranking of feedback formats on accuracy. The 40% of studies that did not report feedback may still have given it. Controlled feedback as a package is promoted via R2/R3; the specific median+rationale recipe remains conventional.
claims.text: Practice guidance says feedback should be quantitative (median, range) plus the recipient's own prior rating; healthcare QI Delphi reports often omit that they gave any between-round feedback at all.

claims.baseline: 76 studies that reported invited panel size (of 80 included)
claims.effect_size: median invited n=17 (Q1=11; Q3=31); min 3, max 418; reported in 76/80 (95%) studies
claims.locator: Table 3 'Number of individuals invited to participate'

source_lineage.authors: Boulkedid R, Abdoul H, Loustau M, Sibony O, Alberti C
source_lineage.title: Using and reporting the Delphi method for selecting healthcare quality indicators: A systematic review

claims.strongest_caveat: Observed medians describe practice, not an accuracy-maximising n. Rowe and Wright (2001) recommend 5-20 as a principle without an isolated n-vs-accuracy experiment in that chapter.
claims.text: Panel-size advice of roughly 5-20 experts is conventional. Boulkedid et al. observed a median invited panel of 17 (Q1 11, Q3 31) in healthcare QI Delphi studies.

claims.baseline: 98 studies that aimed to address consensus
claims.effect_size: 86/98 (87.8%) commented that consensus was reached; only 23/98 (23.5%) stopped primarily because consensus was reached; 70/98 (71.4%) stopped after a specified number of rounds
claims.locator: Table 3; Results section 3.4

source_lineage.title: Defining consensus: A systematic review recommends methodologic criteria for reporting of Delphi studies

claims.strongest_caveat: The review is of published reports, so some studies may have used unreported stopping rules. Of 64 studies with an a priori consensus definition, only 1 (1.5%) stated consensus was not achieved — consistent with consensus being treated as automatic.
claims.text: False or assumed consensus: authors report that consensus was reached even when stopping was not based on a consensus criterion.

claims.baseline: 98 consensus-aiming Delphi studies
claims.effect_size: 26/98 (26.5%) provided no definition; of 72 that did, 21/72 (33%) omitted a threshold; 15 of the 86 'consensus reached' papers had no definition at all
claims.locator: Table 3 'Was consensus defined?'

source_lineage.title: Defining consensus: A systematic review recommends methodologic criteria for reporting of Delphi studies

claims.strongest_caveat: Counts describe published methods sections, not unpublished protocols.
claims.text: Undefined consensus: a substantial minority of Delphi studies never define what would count as agreement, so the output cannot be audited as a statistical group response.

claims.baseline: 80 healthcare quality-indicator Delphi studies
claims.effect_size: only 48/80 (60%) reported feedback between rounds; 32/80 (40%) did not; individual feedback reported in 31/80 (39%)
claims.locator: Abstract and Table 4 Feedback / Individual feedback reported

claims.strongest_caveat: Non-reporting is not proof of non-use. Restricted to healthcare QI Delphi, 1978-2009. Single extractor after a 10-article calibration (median kappa 1).
claims.text: Controlled feedback is omitted or unreported in a large share of applied Delphi studies, so iteration proceeds without the information channel the method claims as its mechanism.

claims.baseline: 73 studies against which the between-round criterion comparison was computed
claims.effect_size: 13/73 (18%) changed selection criteria between rounds
claims.locator: Table 3 footnotes / Discussion paragraph on selection criteria changing between rounds

source_lineage.authors: Boulkedid R, Abdoul H, Loustau M, Sibony O, Alberti C

claims.strongest_caveat: Healthcare QI Delphi only; the 18% is a prevalence, not an accuracy delta.
claims.text: Changing indicator-selection criteria between rounds is equivalent to running a new Delphi; 18% of studies that listed criteria did so, which the reviewers flag as making consensus extremely difficult to interpret.

claims.baseline: 15 included core-outcome-set Delphi studies
claims.effect_size: anonymity clearly reported 4/15 (not clearly 11/15); group feedback method clearly reported 8/15; number completing every round clearly reported 11/15; results for each outcome in each round 0/15; attrition accurately assessable in 11/15
claims.locator: Table 1 reporting-quality items; Results paragraph on attrition

source_lineage.title: Using the Delphi technique to determine which outcomes to measure in clinical trials: recommendations for the future based on a systematic review of existing studies

claims.strongest_caveat: Sinha et al. cite Bardecki (1984) for the causal claim that minority opinions drop out; that 1984 paper was not OA-fetched here, so the causal dropout-of-dissenters story remains E3. This row promotes only the measured reporting failure.
